strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: Clearly identifies and illustrates the fundamental issue of cross-view misalignment in global 3D fusion, proposing a pragmatic local memory alternative with compelling visual evidence (Figure 1).

Clear and practical technical approach: The three-component system (local memory construction, coverage-driven retrieval, multi-anchor weaving) is intuitive, well-explained, and successfully integrated into existing video diffusion models without architectural modifications.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Strong quantitative results (2-5 PSNR improvement), thorough ablation studies validating each design choice, multiple evaluation metrics, and qualitative comparisons across diverse scenes demonstrating consistent improvements.

Solid empirical contributions: Method outperforms strong baselines (Gen3C, TraJCrafter, ViewCrafter, SEVA, Context-as-Memory, SPMem) with consistent gains and shows effective scaling across different backbone architectures (CogVideoX, Wan2.2).
Good presentation quality: Clear writing, informative figures (especially Figures 1-3), well-organized narrative, and effective communication of both motivation and technical approach.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Individual technical components are relatively standard (greedy coverage-based selection, standard transformer attention, learned MLP weighting). Contribution is primarily in system design and combination rather than fundamental innovation.

Artificial and restrictive evaluation scope: Evaluation limited to partial-revisit settings with 70-frame segments, which doesn't reflect challenges of true long-horizon generation. Claims about 'long-horizon consistency' are somewhat overstated given the evaluation scope, and the method's effectiveness on novel scenes beyond revisits is unclear.

Incomplete technical analysis: Missing failure case analysis, computational cost comparisons, memory scaling properties, and error accumulation studies. No clear justification for design choices (e.g., D=8, K=4). Table 3 shows diminishing returns with K but doesn't identify optimal configuration or provide selection guidance.

Methodological limitations: The update-retrieve-generate loop assumes partial generation, limiting zero-shot applicability. Dependency on TTT3R pose/depth estimation without analyzing error propagation. Character masking workaround (Appendix F) appears ad-hoc rather than principled.

Restricted experimental design: Mostly compares against single-anchor methods rather than other memory-augmented approaches. Open-domain examples lack quantitative evaluation and appear potentially cherry-picked. Limited evaluation diversity (primarily RealEstate10K and DL3DV indoor scenes).

Reproducibility and scalability concerns: No code release mentioned, method depends on multiple pre-trained components making full reproduction difficult. Unclear how method scales to truly long sequences (hundreds/thousands of frames) where memory decay becomes critical.

Limited theoretical justification: Primarily empirical work lacking theoretical analysis of when/why local memories outperform global ones, under what conditions each approach is preferable, or formal consistency guarantees.

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine limitations in long-horizon video generation regarding spatial consistency
Intuitive and reasonable approach using localized geometric anchors instead of single global 3D memory
Comprehensive ablation studies examining impact of local vs. global memory, joint vs. separate attention, and number of retrievals
Clear algorithmic description of coverage-driven memory retrieval pipeline with explicit stopping criteria
Extensive qualitative results across diverse scenarios (indoor, outdoor, dynamic scenes) demonstrating practical applicability
Consistent performance improvements over established baselines including GenC, ViewCrafter, TrajCrafter, and SEVA
weaknesses: Core claim about maintaining 'world-consistent' geometry is never quantitatively validated; no metrics measure whether same 3D structures are reconstructed across views
Limited technical novelty - approach primarily combines existing techniques (diffusion models, point cloud retrieval, standard attention) with incremental contribution in memory management
Experimental setting (partial-revisit) is artificial and acknowledged as atypical; most real applications do not revisit earlier frames
Modest quantitative improvements: PSNR/SSIM gains are small (~1-3%), and VBench improvements minimal (~1-2 points); Table 3 shows diminishing returns with more retrievals
Multi-anchor design effectiveness questionable: single-anchor variant (K=1) frequently matches or nearly matches full model, suggesting limited benefit of complexity
Baseline implementation concerns: Context-as-Memory and SPMem had to be re-implemented on different backbone (CogVideoX), introducing implementation bias
Missing failure case analysis, limited discussion of method limitations, and no investigation of when/why the approach succeeds or fails
Coverage-driven retrieval criterion (Section 3.3) lacks theoretical justification - why is coverage maximization the right objective for consistency?
No user studies to validate whether claimed spatial consistency improvements are perceptually meaningful to humans
High computational cost (8×H100 GPUs, ~1 day training) with modest empirical benefits; no inference time comparison with baselines
Limited evaluation scope: only 500 test videos with ~70 frames; primarily indoor scenes; generalization to diverse scenarios unclear
No mention of code availability, limiting reproducibility of this complex multi-component system

strengths: Novel and well-motivated approach replacing global 3D memory with local geometric memories to address cross-view misalignment artifacts in long-horizon video generation
Comprehensive experimental validation with 8 baseline methods, multiple metrics (PSNR, SSIM, VBench), and both partial-revisit and full long-horizon evaluation settings
Rigorous ablation studies systematically demonstrating the contribution of each component (global vs. local memory, pose-conditioning, joint attention, retrieval count)
Consistent quantitative improvements across multiple metrics, particularly on consistency measures (80.98 PSNR vs. 79.66 best baseline)
Exceptional qualitative results showing clear visual advantages over baselines in maintaining spatial consistency and visual quality
Impressive generalization demonstrations including third-person character control, 360-degree panoramic generation, and diverse scene types without retraining
Well-structured presentation with clear visualizations effectively communicating the methodology and results
Detailed implementation details and public datasets enabling reproducibility
weaknesses: Computational cost and runtime complexity not analyzed; overhead from multi-anchor weaving controller and coverage-driven retrieval compared to baselines unknown
Moderate evaluation scale: only 500 training videos and 70 samples for quantitative consistency metrics; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals
Limited theoretical justification for why local memory is fundamentally superior; hyperparameter choices (K=4, coverage threshold=15%) appear empirically driven without principled grounding
Insufficient failure case analysis; edge cases such as complex multi-object scenes, fast camera motion, and occlusions not systematically explored
Dataset-specific training on relatively structured videos (RealEstate10K, DL3DV); generalization to hand-held chaotic camera motion not demonstrated
Incomplete camera control validation; Table 4 compares against Image-to-Video methods rather than camera-control-specific baselines; precise trajectory accuracy not thoroughly validated

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies and demonstrates cross-view misalignment issues with global 3D memory fusion through intuitive visualizations and quantitative analysis

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Extensive comparisons with 8+ baselines, multiple datasets (RealEstate10K, DL3DV), detailed ablation studies (Tables 2-3, Figures 5-6), and analysis of design choices (efficiency scaling, stress testing, failure modes)

Consistent empirical improvements: Table 1 demonstrates meaningful gains in both reconstruction quality (PSNR) and temporal consistency across metrics; visual results clearly show superior consistency with reduced artifacts compared to baselines

Thorough analysis and diagnostics: Section H.1 provides diagnostic analysis explaining why local memories work; Figure 8-9 analyze failure modes; Figure 10 demonstrates superior long-horizon consistency; comprehensive appendices support reproducibility

Practical technical soundness: Coverage-driven retrieval formulation is intuitive; multi-anchor weaving controller reasonably designed with learned pose-proximity weighting; implementation details and algorithm pseudocode facilitate reproduction
Open-domain generalization: Figure 7 demonstrates effective generalization to diverse unseen scenes and camera trajectories, suggesting robustness beyond training distribution
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Core components are straightforward—local point clouds vs. global is a natural modification; coverage-driven retrieval is greedy point-cloud overlap selection without learned mechanisms; multi-anchor controller uses standard transformer layers; minimal novel conceptual contributions

Heavy backbone model dependence: Performance critically depends on underlying video diffusion model; paper doesn't clearly disentangle AnchorWeave contributions from backbone improvements; single-anchor K=1 variant achieves competitive performance with modest ~1-2 dB gains from K=4, questioning whether memory mechanism is the primary driver

Simplistic retrieval mechanism: Algorithm 1 employs basic greedy selection without learned components; thresholds (K=4 retrievals, D=8 chunk length) appear arbitrary; no adaptive selection based on scene complexity; lacks justification for optimality of this specific decomposition

Suboptimal evaluation methodology: Primary reliance on PSNR/SSIM metrics which poorly correlate with perceptual quality in generation tasks; inconsistent perceptual metric reporting (LPIPS, FID); absence of human evaluation studies critical for generation quality; partial-revisit setting may inherently favor the proposed method

Baseline comparison concerns: Some baselines are authors' own re-implementations (Context-as-Memory, SPMem) rather than published code; limited per-baseline analysis of performance gaps; some baselines acknowledged as struggling with out-of-distribution scenarios, potentially creating unfair comparisons

Scalability limitations: 27 seconds for 24-frame generation with 34GB GPU memory (Table 4) impractical for real-time applications; sublinear but still significant scaling; efficiency gains over SPMem not dramatic

Limited theoretical justification: Lacks formal analysis of why local memories fundamentally outperform global fusion beyond avoiding obvious artifacts; pose-weighted importance computation (Section 3.4) insufficiently justified; no convergence analysis

Restricted applicability to dynamic scenes: Acknowledged fundamental limitation to static spatial memories; Section H.3's masking strategy is a workaround rather than principled solution; significantly limits applicability to truly dynamic environments

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies and illustrates how global 3D reconstruction introduces cross-view misalignment artifacts in long-horizon video generation
Reasonable core approach: Using local per-frame point cloud memories instead of global reconstruction is intuitive and well-justified

Comprehensive experimental framework: Includes quantitative metrics (PSNR, SSIM, consistency), ablations on key components, efficiency analysis, and diverse evaluation scenarios (partial-revisit and free-form control)
Detailed methodology: Clear descriptions of local memory construction (Section 3.2), coverage-driven retrieval (Section 3.3), and multi-anchor weaving controller (Section 3.4)
Extensive qualitative evaluation: Thorough visual comparisons with multiple baselines and honest discussion of failure modes (reflections, long-horizon drift, dynamic content) in Section I
Technically sound implementation: Standard but properly executed components including COLMAP-based geometry, diffusion backbone integration, and attention mechanisms
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Coverage-driven retrieval is essentially a greedy field-of-view overlap algorithm; multi-anchor controller uses standard cross-attention; core contribution (local vs. global memory) is incremental relative to prior memory-augmented generation work

Modest quantitative improvements without statistical rigor: Table 1 shows gains of ~1-2 dB PSNR and ~0.01-0.03 SSIM; improvements fall within expected variance margins for complex generation; no confidence intervals, p-values, or user studies provided

Significant experimental methodology concerns: (1) Baselines re-implemented rather than using official code, introducing confounds; (2) Modified training protocols for baselines not fully detailed; (3) Test set limited to ~70 frames per video, not truly 'long-horizon'; (4) Partial-revisit evaluation inherently favors retrieval-based methods

Missing theoretical and design justifications: No ablation for why controller injected at 1/3 of layers; coverage metric (FoV overlap) may not correlate with visual consistency; diminishing returns with K unexplained; joint attention benefits over independent processing unanalyzed

Limited generalization: Training exclusively on structured indoor scenes (RealEstate10K, DL3DV); 'open-domain' examples still controlled with keyboard-driven cameras; no evaluation on dynamic content, fast motion, or truly unconstrained scenarios; unclear out-of-distribution performance

Scalability and efficiency trade-offs not justified: Memory scales linearly with history (Figure 8), reaching 39GB at K=4; overhead over simpler baselines (SPMem: 30GB) does not clearly justify added complexity given modest gains

Complex method obscures core contribution: Multiple interacting components (local memory, coverage retrieval, joint attention, pose conditioning) make it difficult to isolate which elements drive improvements; unclear which design choices are critical

Incomplete ablations: Table 2 lacks temporal consistency metrics for global vs. local comparison; no ablation isolating joint attention benefit; K ablation doesn't explain plateau or justify stopping at K=4

Unresolved known limitations: Acknowledges reflective surfaces and dynamic content as hard problems but offers no algorithmic advances beyond the local memory idea; these remain fundamental challenges

Incongruent results with claims: Table 5 shows camera control error (0.61) slightly worse than some baselines, contradicting narrative that local geometry improves camera following; K=1 sometimes underperforms baselines suggesting joint controller isn't uniformly beneficial

strengths: Clear problem motivation: Effectively articulates the fundamental limitation of global 3D reconstruction approaches (cross-view misalignment) and proposes an intuitive solution via local geometric memories.

Novel technical contribution: The integration of local spatial anchors, coverage-driven retrieval, and multi-anchor weaving controller is well-designed and each component is justified through ablations.

Strong empirical results: Achieves best overall performance on RealEstate10K and DL3DV, with particularly impressive long-horizon consistency (~20dB PSNR at 1000 frames) and better camera controllability than baselines.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple baselines, thorough ablations (Tables 2-3, Figures 5-6), evaluation on two backbones, and both quantitative and qualitative assessments demonstrate experimental rigor.
Excellent presentation and reproducibility: Clear methodology, informative visualizations (especially Figures 1-3, 6), detailed implementation in appendices, and honest discussion of limitations.
Practical algorithmic design: Coverage-driven memory retrieval (Algorithm 1) provides an efficient, principled approach to selecting informative anchors without manual tuning.
Stress testing and robustness analysis: Extended evaluations including 2400-frame trajectories (Figure 10), open-domain generalization (Figure 7), and detailed failure mode analysis (Appendix H).
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope: Only two similar datasets (RealEstate10K, DL3DV) evaluated; lacks assessment on established video benchmarks, diverse camera motions, or significantly different environment types.

Computational overhead: Moderate but non-trivial overhead (Table 4: 275s vs 221s); memory requirements for storing local point clouds and retrieval process not fully characterized relative to sequence length.
Dependence on initialization quality: Method requires pre-estimated poses and initial frames; robustness to pose errors not quantified or ablated, potentially limiting real-world applicability.
Fundamental limitations with dynamic content: Dynamic object handling requires manual masking (Section H.3); scalability to highly dynamic scenes unclear and somewhat ad-hoc.
Baseline comparison fairness: Context-as-Memory and SPMem reimplemented rather than official; K=1 comparisons may not be ideal since baselines weren't designed for multi-anchor retrieval.
Unresolved failure modes: Reflective surfaces (Figure 13) remain problematic; view-dependent effects fundamentally cannot be captured by static point clouds, with no proposed solution.

Limited novelty in individual components: Local geometric anchors and multi-anchor attention are conceptually straightforward; primary novelty lies in their combination rather than fundamental algorithmic innovation.

Generalization questions: Open-domain examples use manually specified smooth trajectories; unclear how method performs with erratic camera motion or truly free-form interaction beyond demonstrated scenarios.

Technical clarity gaps: Camera pose encoding in controller underspecified; notation inconsistencies (K used for both maximum and actual retrievals); insufficient detail on why certain design choices (e.g., FFD for initialization) are superior.
